Sort the elements as a_1 < … < a_n with n = 2025. I derived the answer independently by computing each element's weight in P − Q.

**Weights.** The element a_i is the median of an odd subset of size 2k+1 exactly when k smaller and k larger elements are chosen. By Vandermonde, its total weight in P is Σ_k C(i−1,k)·C(n−i,k) = C(2024, i−1).

It is the median of an even subset of size 2k when k−1 smaller and k larger elements are chosen, since the median is then the lower of the two middle elements (the problem does not specify which middle convention is used for even sets). Its total weight in Q is Σ_k C(i−1,k−1)·C(n−i,k) = C(2024, i).

So P − Q = Σ w_i·a_i with w_i = C(2024, i−1) − C(2024, i).

**Abel summation.** The tail sums telescope: Σ_{i≥j} w_i = C(2024, j−1) − C(2024, 2025) = C(2024, j−1). With d_1 = a_1 and d_i = a_i − a_{i−1} > 0, this gives P − Q = Σ C(2024, i−1)·d_i. Since Σ d_i = max(A), we get P − Q ≤ max_i C(2024, i−1) · max(A), and the maximum is C(2024, 1012).

**Tightness.** Put almost all the gap at d_1013: take a_1, …, a_1012 near 0 and a_1013, …, a_2025 near max(A). This approaches the bound, so C = C(2024, 1012).

**Small-case check.** For n = 3 the weights are −1, 1, 1, so the supremum is 2 = C(2,1). This matches the formula.

**Solution 1:** It assumes the extremal sets use only the values 0 and 1 and gets a different formula. The true weights are binomial coefficients applied to the gaps, so the answer is C(2024, 1012), not this expression. Wrong.

**Solution 2:** It claims 1012 using a configuration that is not extremal. Taking a_1 → 0 and the rest equal to 1 gives weight C(2024, 1) − … only partially, and the true supremum is far larger. Wrong.

**Solution 3:** It matches my derivation and its answer is C(2024, 1012). Correct.
